analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal bureau empowered to cap prescription drug prices at international levels and license patents if companies refuse.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Health committee, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new government bureau inside the Department of Health and Human Services that reviews the prices of prescription drugs and decides whether each price is "appropriate." Drug companies would have to disclose detailed information about their research costs, marketing, patents, executive pay, and prices abroad. For many drugs, the bureau would set a ceiling based on the median price charged in 11 other wealthy countries, and companies charging above it would have to lower prices and return the extra money to patients. Companies that refused could lose their exclusive rights to the drug, letting the government authorize other manufacturers to produce it. The bill would also repeal a Medicare provision that bars the government from getting directly involved in drug price negotiations.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay out of pocket for brand-name prescription drugs, including uninsured people and people on Medicare and Medicaid, would pay less when prices are capped at international levels. Taxpayers would also benefit, because Medicare and Medicaid would spend less on overpriced drugs.

how_it_helps.text: For a large class of drugs, the Bureau would set an interim maximum price equal to the median list price in countries like Canada, Germany, France, Japan, and the UK, and order manufacturers to charge no more than that [S2].

If a company raises its price faster than inflation, the price would automatically be deemed not appropriate unless the Bureau found it justified, and excess revenue would have to be remitted and distributed to affected patients [S2].

Manufacturers would have to disclose clinical trial costs per trial, marketing spending, patent portfolios, executive compensation, federal subsidies received, and their prices abroad — information now kept confidential [S2].

Companies that refuse to lower a price deemed too high would lose exclusive rights, allowing others to manufacture the drug at the approved price with reasonable compensation to the original maker; the bill also repeals Medicare's noninterference clause, which currently prohibits the government from negotiating prices directly [S2].

Patients could petition the Bureau directly about drug prices, and a Consumer Advisory Council dominated by patient representatives would oversee the work; bureau staff would be barred from having conflicts of interest [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost through capped prices, required refunds of excess revenue, penalties of at least 150% of excess revenues, and possible loss of patent exclusivity. Taxpayers would fund the new Bureau at $50 million per year. If price caps reduce drug-company revenues, that could mean less investment in new drug development over time.

drawbacks.text: Caps tied to foreign list prices and forced patent licensing could reduce the revenue that funds pharmaceutical research, which the industry argues would slow development of new medicines [S2].

The interim price ceiling would apply immediately and broadly to most brand-name drugs not facing generic competition, without individual review first — a design that could hit legitimately high-cost drugs alongside overpriced ones [S2].

The bill creates a permanent $50 million-per-year federal agency and grants it sweeping power to review and set prices for any prescription drug, which critics would call an unprecedented level of government price control [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing the highest drug prices in the world, the direct benefits are large and immediate: capped prices, refunds, and a direct line to the regulator. The main cost is uncertain but real — lower drug-company profits could mean less research on future medicines, and the immediate blanket price cap skips individual case-by-case review. Whether the trade is worth it depends heavily on how much of current drug pricing reflects genuine development costs versus market power.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Booker introduced the bill in July 2024, but the Senate Health committee never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker, joined by Sen. Bernie Sanders, introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability and Access Act on July 30, 2024 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — its only action besides introduction [S4].
One Independent senator cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or Republican beyond the sponsors signed on, and no further committee action was recorded before the Congress ended [S3].
Under Senate rules, a bill that its committee never reports out cannot reach the floor, so the bill expired without any vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: they keep their current pricing power, and no new price caps, disclosure requirements, or patent-licensing penalties were enacted.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee chair
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsor (the bill's 1 of 4 Senate Independent cosponsor)

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the record shows no opposition votes — only that support never grew beyond one Democrat and one Independent senator, and the committee (chaired by a cosponsor) never acted.

industries.note: The bill would cap their prices at median foreign prices, force refunds of excess revenue, impose penalties up to 150% of excess revenues, and authorize others to make their drugs if they refuse to comply. It would also end the Medicare ban on direct government negotiation.

The bill would require disclosure of PBM rebate and net-price arrangements and repeal Medicare's noninterference clause, threatening the rebate-driven business model that sits between manufacturers and patients.

If a brand manufacturer refuses to lower a price deemed too high, the government could authorize other entities to manufacture the drug at the approved price, creating new generic and biosimilar production opportunities.
Medicare and Medicaid would spend less on drugs whose prices are deemed not appropriate, reducing government drug expenditures.
